Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: Duke is the opposite of a Rule Breaker: a century-old regulated utility in a mature industry, with a monopoly granted by regulators rather than earned through innovation. Its share price fell about 2% over the past year and it trades at a modest 18-19x earnings, so it lacks the momentum and 'overvalued' label Gardner likes; the data-center power boom is its only emerging-trend angle.
summaries.buffett: Duke is simple to understand, has an enduring regulated franchise and has paid a dividend for 100 consecutive years, all things Buffett values (Berkshire itself owns regulated utilities). But returns on capital are low (ROIC about 3.8%), free cash flow is negative because capex ($14,024M in 2025) exceeds operating cash flow, and debt is heavy at $91.2B, so it fits his utility template rather than his ideal high-return compounder.
summaries.munger: Munger would see an understandable, durable monopoly with few ways to fail outright, but also a capital-hungry business whose returns are capped by regulators. With ROIC near 3.8%, negative free cash flow and reliance on debt and equity issuance, it is a 'fair business at a fair price' rather than a great business.
summaries.lynch: Duke is a classic Lynch 'slow grower'/stalwart: big, well known, paying a 3.5% dividend with 5-7% EPS growth targeted through 2030. Its P/E of about 18.7 is roughly three times its earnings growth rate, so it fails his PEG test, and with 71% institutional ownership it is not overlooked.
summaries.fisher: Fisher looked for companies with large sales-growth potential driven by R&D and sales skill; Duke grows only as fast as regulators allow it to invest (revenue up about 3.9% a year over 2022-2025). Management is competent and candid, but the business does not develop new products or rely on R&D, so it fits Fisher's approach poorly.
summaries.graham: Duke passes several defensive-investor tests: it is large, profitable every year for the last decade, has paid dividends for 100 consecutive years, and EPS rose from $4.05 in 2015 to $6.31 in 2025. It fails on price (about 24x three-year average earnings and P/E x P/B of roughly 34) and on financial strength (current ratio about 0.66, heavy debt).
summaries.thiel: Duke has a monopoly, but it is a legal franchise rather than one built on proprietary technology, and its market is mature and regulated. It scores well on durability and distribution (it already serves 8.7 million electric customers) but poorly on technology, secret insight and founder-led ambition.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner favours fast-growing companies with strong unit economics benefiting from big platform shifts; Duke benefits indirectly from the AI data-center build-out (7.8 GW signed, 15.4 GW late-stage pipeline) but grows revenue only about 4-5% a year with negative free cash flow. It would be at best a defensive, rate-sensitive holding in his framework.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller trades on liquidity, rates and earnings momentum; Duke's earnings are steady (six straight EPS beats) but not accelerating sharply, and as a heavily indebted utility it is hurt by higher interest rates. The data-center power demand story is a real catalyst, but the stock's flat past year shows little momentum.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital, high margins and cash generation without leverage; Duke earns ROIC near 3.8%, has negative free cash flow and debt of about $91B, so it fails his 'good company' test despite its predictable demand.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Duke ranks poorly: operating income of $8,626M is only about 4.6% of its roughly $188B enterprise value, and its return on tangible capital is low because utility assets are huge.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, great managers and great reinvestment opportunities. Duke has huge reinvestment opportunities ($103B five-year capital plan) and capable management, but each dollar reinvested earns only regulated returns (a 9.8% allowed ROE in North Carolina), so the business leg is weak.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks simple, distressed businesses with low downside and high upside; Duke is simple with low risk of permanent loss, but it is neither distressed nor cheap and its upside is limited by regulated returns.
summaries.wood: Duke is not a disruptive-innovation company: it does not lead in AI, robotics, storage or other ARK platforms, though it supplies power to AI data centers. Cathie Wood's framework would not favour it.
summaries.ackman: Ackman likes simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating businesses with high barriers to entry; Duke is simple, predictable and protected by regulation, but generates negative free cash flow and depends on interest rates and regulators, which Ackman tries to avoid.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economies shared' model is partly echoed in a regulated utility that passes cost savings to customers through rates, but Duke has no compounding flywheel or rising market share. Its future position looks stable, not clearly stronger, so it fits his approach only loosely.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine sought huge, fast-growing markets created by new technology, backed by start-ups; Duke is a mature, regulated incumbent. It solves an essential problem (reliable power) but has nothing of the venture profile he looked for.
summaries.nash: Duke fails most of Tom Nash's quantitative tests: revenue grows about 6% a year, debt ($91.2B) dwarfs cash ($673M), free cash flow is negative and interest coverage is about 2.4x. It does sell into the energy/AI-power secular trend and beats earnings estimates consistently, scoring about 70 of 130 on his 13 categories.

momentum.evidence: The share price fell about 2.3% over the past 52 weeks to $124.98 (Oct 23, 2026), lagging the market.

g4.evidence: CEO Harry Sideris is a 29-year company veteran with solid execution, and Brookfield agreed to invest $6 billion for a 19.7% stake in Duke Energy Florida, but the company is not backed by famous investors.

g6.evidence: At about 18.7x trailing earnings with an average analyst target of $132 (5.7% upside), commentators do not commonly call it overvalued.

simple.evidence: It sells regulated electricity and gas to about 8.7 million electric and 1.6 million gas customers in six states; the model is simple to understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $23,366M (2020) to $32,237M (2025), and it has paid a cash dividend for 100 consecutive years.

integrity.evidence: Management gives clear guidance (5-7% EPS growth through 2030) and has beaten EPS estimates six straight quarters, but insiders own only about 0.12% and capital allocation is driven by regulated rate-base growth.

b6.evidence: Duke has narrowed to fully regulated utilities (selling commercial renewables and Piedmont's Tennessee gas business), but its $103B capital plan is the kind of rate-base expansion all peers pursue.

roic.evidence: ROIC is only about 3.8% and ROE about 9.9%, and returns depend on heavy debt ($91,238M at June 30, 2026).

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow is negative: 2025 operating cash flow of $12,330M was below capital expenditures of $14,024M.

b10.evidence: EPS rose from $4.05 in 2015 to $6.31 in 2025, but the stock's 10-year return of about 127% trailed the S&P 500's 258%.

safety.evidence: At $124.98 it trades at about 18.7x trailing earnings and 1.8x book with negative free cash flow, offering no clear margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 18.3 is in line with regulated utility peers for 5-7% EPS growth plus a 3.5% dividend, but it is not cheap.

mu5.evidence: As a regulated monopoly providing essential power, it has few paths to outright failure; the main risks are adverse regulation, storms and financing costs.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest for many years (a $103B 2026-2030 capital plan driving 9.6% earnings-base growth), but only at regulated returns around a 9.8% ROE.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear stalwart/slow grower: a large utility targeting 5-7% annual EPS growth through 2030 plus a dividend.

ly3.evidence: The P/E of about 18.7 is far above its 5-7% targeted EPS growth rate (PEG about 2.8).

runway.evidence: Data-center demand (7.8 GW signed, 15.4 GW late-stage pipeline) and 1.4% customer growth support steady growth, but it cannot expand beyond its regulated territories.

ly7.evidence: Insiders own about 0.12% and the share count rose about 0.4% year on year as Duke issues equity (e.g. $600M priced under its ATM program in 2026).

ly8.evidence: With about 71% institutional ownership and coverage by over 20 analysts, it is widely followed, even if utilities are considered 'boring'.

fi2.evidence: Duke is adding new generation (15 GW of new capacity by 2031, evaluating AP1000 and SMR nuclear) but does not develop new products in Fisher's sense.

fi3.evidence: Duke does not report material R&D spending, so its R&D productivity cannot be judged.

fi4.evidence: As a regulated monopoly it does not need or show unusual sales skill, although it has won large data-center and economic-development projects (about $5 billion of investment in the first half of 2026).

longterm.evidence: It invests for decades (nuclear life extensions to 80 years, a $103B capital plan), though its focus is regulated earnings growth rather than innovation.

gr1.evidence: A Fortune 150 company with $32,237M of 2025 revenue and about $97B market cap.

ni10.evidence: It has reported positive GAAP earnings every year from 2016 ($3.11 EPS) through 2025 ($6.31 EPS), including a low of $1.72 in 2020.

gr4.evidence: Duke has paid a cash dividend on its common stock for 100 consecutive years (July 2026 release).

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $4.05 in 2015 to $6.31 in 2025, an increase of about 56%.

gr6.evidence: At $124.98 the price is about 24x the 2023-2025 average diluted EPS of $5.19.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 18.7 times P/B of about 1.8 gives roughly 34, above Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: Duke has no proprietary technology; it runs standard nuclear, gas, hydro and solar plants and grid equipment.

timing.evidence: Timing is good for demand (data centers, reshoring), but high interest rates and turbine and supply-chain constraints raise costs.

th3.evidence: It did not start small; it is a long-established incumbent utility serving entire regions.

team.evidence: Sideris and team are experienced utility operators who have delivered results, but not an exceptional founder-led team.

th5.evidence: It already has a direct billing relationship with 8.7 million electric and 1.6 million gas customers.

durable.evidence: Its regulated franchises and grid assets are likely to remain essential in 10-20 years, though rooftop solar and batteries pose some long-term risk.

th7.evidence: Its opportunities (data-center load, gas and nuclear build-out) are widely seen by all large utilities.

trend.evidence: It benefits from AI data-center power demand (7.8 GW signed agreements), but as a supplier to that trend rather than a leader of it.

dr1.evidence: Adjusted EPS grew from $1.25 to $1.43 in Q2 2026 and 2026 guidance of $6.55-6.80 implies growth, but consensus earnings growth is steady (about 8% a year) rather than accelerating.

dr2.evidence: Pending North Carolina rate orders, Brookfield's Florida proceeds and conversion of the 15.4 GW pipeline by 1H 2027 could improve the picture, but much of this is already in guidance.

dr4.evidence: As a heavily indebted utility (interest coverage about 2.4x), higher rates and tight credit work against it; falling rates would help.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include North Carolina rate case orders expected by mid-November 2026, conversion of the 15.4 GW data-center pipeline and a possible $5-10B addition to the capital plan.

dr7.evidence: Its low-growth, regulated profile and heavy leverage make it a poor candidate for a large concentrated position in a momentum-driven approach.

gm.evidence: Revenue less fuel and purchased power was 75.0% of revenue in 2025, though this reflects regulated cost pass-through rather than pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: Free cash flow is negative (TTM about -$4.3B, a -4.4% yield).

gb2.evidence: Operating income of $8,626M is only about 4.6% of its roughly $188B enterprise value.

pa2.evidence: It is not in a temporary setback; results are steady and growing.

pa4.evidence: Its regulated monopoly and essential service make permanent loss of capital unlikely, though high leverage and regulation are risks.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics, though it builds batteries and supplies power to AI data centers.

wo2.evidence: Its costs are rising, not falling, with large new generation and grid investments.

wo3.evidence: It is a single-platform regulated utility.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market is its regulated territories; consensus sees revenue growing to about $37.1B by 2028, not many times larger.

ac3.evidence: It is exposed to interest rates (about $91B of debt), fuel prices (largely passed through) and regulatory decisions.

ns1.evidence: Regulation forces cost savings to flow back to customers through rates (e.g. accelerated tax-credit flow-back in Florida), but this does not deepen a competitive moat.

ns4.evidence: Data-center growth and a larger rate base should make it bigger in 10-20 years, but its competitive position is fixed by regulation rather than clearly stronger.

va2.evidence: Reliable electricity and gas is a large, essential need for millions of homes and businesses.

tn1.evidence: It sells into the energy-for-AI secular trend as infrastructure, but it is an old utility adapting rather than a company built for that trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees it as a regulated utility, which is what it is becoming too; no big narrative gap.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap US company and not in Nash's avoid zones (it is not a commodity producer, airline, Chinese stock or startup).

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three (revenue grew every year 2020-2025 and it is profitable) but has far more debt ($91.2B) than cash ($673M), which utility infrastructure leverage only partly excuses.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been negative and debt has exceeded cash in each recent quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 6.2% in 2025 and consensus expects about 4.7% in 2026.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about 6% plus a negative free-cash-flow margin is far below 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue grew 6.2% ($30,357M to $32,237M) while total operating expenses grew 5.3% ($22,431M to $23,611M).

tn9.evidence: It hits instant kills: more debt than cash and revenue growth below 10%.

tn10.evidence: No existential legal threat, but its prices and returns depend on state regulators, with North Carolina rate orders pending and affordability scrutiny rising.

tn11.evidence: Duke provides electricity and gas that keep homes and businesses running in six states, charging regulated rates per kWh and therm; customers use it because it is the franchise provider.

tn13.evidence: Score about 70: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 10 (26.8%), short interest 10 (2.3%), institutional ownership 10 (71%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 0 (40% vs 72%), moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture/mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year 2020-2025, but operating margin dipped in 2022, free cash flow was negative throughout and debt always exceeded cash.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 2.4x, the current ratio about 0.66, and total liabilities (about $144B) are more than 2.5x equity of $56.9B; it fails the coverage and current-ratio tests.

tn18.evidence: Sideris has executed well since April 2025 (six straight EPS beats under Duke), but he has been CEO for only about 1.5 years, is not a founder and has no notable open-market purchases.

tn20.evidence: Adjusted EPS beat consensus in all six quarters from Q1 2025 to Q2 2026 (average surprise about +6%).

tn21.evidence: No red flags: a single CEO, no acquisition spree, no accounting concerns, Deloitte remains auditor, and operating margins have risen.

tn22.evidence: It has $32B of revenue, steady profits and no hype, though it does issue some equity to fund capex.

tn24.evidence: With negative free cash flow, today's price implies growth that relies on future rate-base returns rather than cash the company is already generating.

tn25.evidence: With negative free-cash-flow margins, Nash's DCF gives a value well below the $124.98 price at a 12% discount rate.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 18.3 is in line with peers, but the PEG of about 2.8 is well above 1.
